Steps to Take Following a Motorcycle Crash in Fort Collins
The decisions a rider makes in the minutes and days after a crash often shape the outcome of the entire claim. There are a few key things to
know to file a motorcycle crash claim
, starting with medical care, which always comes first, even when injuries seem minor at the scene, since adrenaline can mask the early signs of a fracture or head injury.
Once treatment begins, a few additional steps help protect both health and legal options:
Request a copy of the police report
Photograph the scene and any visible injuries
Collect contact information from witnesses before they leave
Preserve damaged gear, like a helmet or jacket, since it shows impact force
Avoid detailed statements to insurance adjusters until speaking with an attorney
Contact a
Fort Collins motorcycle accident lawyer
before providing a recorded statement

Insurance adjusters may call within days of a crash, and statements made during those calls can be used to minimize a claim later on. Many of the same steps to take after a crash apply to riders and drivers alike, and taking them early protects a rider from having to make decisions while still recovering.

Riding Conditions and Motorcycle Safety in Fort Collins

Fort Collins has seen a steady rise in motorcycle traffic each riding season. Once the weather warms up, riders fill College Avenue, Harmony Road, and the I-25 corridor alongside daily commuters, and more riders on the road means more chances for a crash. The most recent available data clearly reflects that risk.
The
Colorado Department of Transportation

reported a record 165 motorcycle deaths in Colorado in 2024, nearly one in every four traffic deaths statewide, even though motorcycles make up only three percent of registered vehicles. In 2025, the number dropped slightly to 147 deaths. Still, warm weather in November and December caused a sharp spike in late-season crashes compared with the same months in 2024.

Helmets remain one of the biggest factors in survival. In Colorado, nearly half of all motorcyclists killed in the past five years did not wear a helmet. Colorado also passed a new law in 2024, letting motorcycles slowly filter between stopped vehicles in traffic. Every Fort Collins driver and rider should understand this law before merging or changing lanes near a motorcycle.
Frequent Causes of Motorcycle Crashes in Fort Collins, Colorado

Those same conditions, heavy seasonal traffic, unfamiliar laws, and crowded intersections, help explain why certain crash patterns repeat across Fort Collins. Most collisions trace back to a driver who failed to see or account for a rider sharing the road. Our
Fort Collins motorcycle accident lawyers
review these patterns closely, since the cause of a crash often determines who bears responsibility.
Common causes may include:
Left-turn collisions, where a driver misjudges a motorcycle’s speed or distance and turns into its path
Distracted driving, particularly when a driver glances at a phone or dashboard display near a merge point
Unsafe lane changes and failure to check blind spots, especially during peak commuter hours near I-25
Tailgating and following a motorcycle too closely to react in time
Hazardous roadway conditions, including loose gravel, potholes, and poorly marked construction zones
Identifying the specific cause of a crash often determines which party or parties bear legal responsibility for an injured rider’s damages.
Types of Injuries Caused by Motorcycle Crashes

Behind every one of these causes is a rider left exposed to forces a car’s frame would normally absorb. Motorcycles offer none of the structural protection a car provides, and the injuries that follow a crash reflect that vulnerability.
Common injuries include
Traumatic brain injuries, ranging from a mild concussion to lasting cognitive impairment
Spinal cord injuries, which can affect mobility and require extended rehabilitation
Multiple fractures, often requiring surgery and months of recovery
Severe road rash
, which can cause permanent scarring and infection
Internal organ damage, which can go unnoticed right after a crash

Prompt medical evaluation matters regardless of how a rider feels immediately after a crash, since some injuries may take hours or days to fully surface. The severity of these injuries shapes both the medical treatment a rider needs and the value of any resulting injury claim.
Recovering Compensation After a Fort Collins Motorcycle Accident
Building a strong case means accounting for every loss a crash creates, and it’s where
Dormer Harpring
focuses its work on behalf of injured riders. Injured riders in Colorado may pursue compensation for several types of losses, including:
Medical expenses, including emergency care, surgery, and ongoing treatment
Future medical costs for injuries requiring long-term care, such as traumatic brain injuries or spinal damage
Lost wages from time away from work during recovery
Reduced earning capacity if an injury affects a rider’s ability to work long-term
Pain and suffering tied to the physical and emotional impact of the crash
Property damage for the repair or replacement of the motorcycle and gear
Punitive damages, awarded in cases of especially reckless conduct, meant to punish rather than compensate
A
settlement
accepted too early rarely accounts for costs that emerge months or years later, which is why full documentation of both current and future needs matters before agreeing to any offer.
Colorado also follows a modified comparative negligence rule under
Colorado Revised Statutes Section 13-21-111

. Under this rule, an injured rider can recover damages as long as they are found less at fault than the other party, though any compensation is reduced by their percentage of fault. Insurance companies often try to shift blame onto the rider to reduce or deny a claim, which is why a thorough investigation, including witness statements and roadway evidence, matters to protecting its full value.
Time Limits for Pursuing a Motorcycle Accident Case in Fort Collins
Full recovery depends on acting within the window Colorado law allows. Under
Colorado Revised Statutes Section 13-80-101
, injured riders generally have three years from the date of the crash to
file a motorcycle accident claim
, and missing that deadline can permanently end a rider’s right to compensation.

However, exceptions may apply depending on the circumstances of a case, such as crashes involving a government vehicle, a minor, or an injury discovered well after the crash occurred. Evidence also disappears quickly, from fading skid marks to overwritten surveillance footage, so consulting a
Fort Collins motorcycle accident lawyer
earlier helps preserve what a claim depends on and gives an attorney time to build the case before the deadline arrives.
Colorado Motorcycle Laws That May Affect Your Claim
Filing on time matters, but a few other Colorado laws can also shape how a claim plays out. Here is what riders should know:
Helmet Use:
Riders 18 and older can legally ride without a helmet, but going without one can become a point of dispute if an insurer argues it worsened injuries, a common tactic under Colorado’s
comparative negligence
rule.
Lane Filtering:
A 2024 law allows motorcycles to move slowly between stopped vehicles in traffic. Confusion about this law among drivers still contributes to some collisions.
Minimum Insurance Requirements:
Colorado requires drivers to carry liability coverage, but the state minimum often falls short of covering the costs of a serious motorcycle injury.
Uninsured and Underinsured Motorist Coverage:
This coverage is often essential when the at-fault driver carries only the state minimum coverage or no insurance at all.
Understanding how these laws apply to a specific crash often shapes whether a settlement fully accounts for a rider’s actual losses.

faqs.question: Can I file a claim if I was not wearing a helmet?

children.text: Yes, helmet use is optional in Colorado for riders eighteen and older, and going without one does not automatically bar a claim. An insurer may still try to argue it increased the severity of an injury, which is why documentation and legal guidance matter.

faqs.question: What if I was a passenger on the motorcycle, not the rider?

children.text: Passengers can pursue their own claim independent of the rider’s, particularly when the driver of another vehicle caused the crash. A passenger’s right to compensation does not depend on which party operated the motorcycle.

faqs.question: How long does a motorcycle accident case typically take to resolve?

children.text: Timelines vary based on the severity of the injury and whether liability is disputed. Straightforward cases with clear fault may be resolved in months, while cases involving serious or long-term injuries often take longer to ensure the full extent of damages is properly documented.
